title: Pink Ball in Day Tests. Coaches on the Field. Hawk-Eye for Umpires. The ICC Has Rewritten the Rules.
excerpt: The Ahmedabad Board meeting approved a wave of changes to how cricket is played, officiated, and coached — from ball colour in Tests to 15-minute T20I innings breaks.
body:
The ICC Board meetings in Ahmedabad concluded on Sunday with a set of decisions that will reshape how international cricket is played, coached, and governed. The changes, approved following recommendations from the Chief Executives Committee, touch everything from the colour of the ball in Test matches to the role of technology in policing bowling actions.

## Pink Ball in Day Tests

The most headline-grabbing change is the approval of a trial allowing the pink ball to be used in regular Test matches — not just day-night games — when both teams agree, to maximise play in conditions where bad light would otherwise stop the game.

Until now, the pink ball has been reserved for day-night Tests, where it is used under floodlights. The new trial acknowledges a persistent problem in Test cricket: lost overs due to fading light, particularly in England, where twilight conditions routinely shave hours off the final sessions.

Both teams must agree before the ball is switched. It is a trial, not a permanent rule change, and the ICC will assess the impact before deciding whether to make it standard.

Alongside the pink ball trial, the ICC announced co-funding of research with the Marylebone Cricket Club into lighting technology for match officials and venues, aimed at further reducing the play lost to poor light.

## Coaches Enter the Field

Head coaches will now be allowed to consult with their teams during scheduled drinks intervals in ODI matches — a right already granted in T20Is. The change formalises what many teams were already doing informally and gives coaches a direct tactical role during play.

The amendment also applies to any designated coach representative, not just the head coach. Whether coaches will need to wear team jerseys to step onto the field remains to be clarified.

## Shorter T20I Innings Breaks

The T20I innings break has been cut from 20 minutes to 15 minutes. The change is aimed at tightening match schedules and maintaining broadcast momentum — a clear nod to the commercial realities of the shortest format.

Teams will have five fewer minutes to regroup, strategise, and recover between innings. For NRI fans watching from the United States and Canada, where T20I broadcasts are timed to fit weekday evening slots, the shorter break is a practical improvement.

## Hawk-Eye for Bowling Actions

In a significant technological shift, match officials will now be able to access Hawk-Eye data when considering whether to report a bowler for a suspect action. Previously, officials relied on the naked eye and slow-motion replays to identify illegal actions.

The integration of Hawk-Eye — which can measure the exact degree of arm extension and flexion — gives umpires a data-driven tool that could reduce both false reports and missed offenders.

## Other Changes

The ICC also approved the permanent adoption of the leg-side wides trial, which has been running successfully for several seasons. All remaining MCC Laws of Cricket changes will be adopted effective October 1, 2026. And in women’s cricket, the ICC Women’s Champions Trophy 2027 has been moved from its June-July window to February 14–28, 2027.

## Franchise Cricket Under Scrutiny

The Board expressed concern about the growing expanse of franchise cricket leagues and resolved to form a committee to assess how franchise cricket can be harmonised with the international calendar. With the IPL, BBL, PSL, SA20, ILT20, and MLC all competing for player availability, the committee’s findings could have far-reaching implications for how cricket is scheduled globally.

“Our discussions in Ahmedabad have reinforced the ICC’s commitment to governance, administration and the growth of cricket globally,” ICC Chairman Jay Shah said.

For Indian cricket fans — and the millions of diaspora followers who follow the game across multiple formats and time zones — the Ahmedabad decisions signal that the ICC is willing to evolve. Whether these changes will be enough to keep Test cricket relevant and franchise cricket manageable is the question that will define the next decade of the sport.
